parts.title: Where did the local chickens of the Middle East, North Africa and the Horn of Africa come from? Tracing their mothers' family lines
parts.abstract:
Background

Local, or "indigenous", chickens are a major source of protein for farming communities around the world. In the Middle East and Africa, these chickens are suited to hot, dry and fairly dry areas. Their wild ancestor, the Red junglefowl, lives in damp tropical areas instead. As people want more chicken meat and eggs, these local chickens are becoming fewer, because farmers are turning to foreign commercial breeds that produce more.

In this paper, we ask where the chickens of the Middle East (Iraq and Saudi Arabia), of northern Africa (Algeria and Libya) and of the Horn of Africa (Ethiopia) came from, and which routes they travelled along. To answer this, we read a short stretch of DNA called the D-loop. It is found in the mitochondria, the tiny energy-making parts of a cell, and it is passed down only from mothers to their young. This makes it a good way to trace a chicken's mother's family line.

Results

We studied the D-loop in 706 chicken samples: 107 from Iraq, 185 from Saudi Arabia, 88 from Algeria, 23 from Libya, 211 from Ethiopia and 92 from Pakistan. We found five haplogroups, which are family branches of related DNA versions, named A, B, C, D and E. This suggests that the chickens we studied came from more than one mother's origin.

Haplogroup E turned up in 625 samples and was the most common in every country. It most likely comes from the Indian subcontinent (the part of Asia that includes India and Pakistan), and it probably reached these countries by land. Haplogroup D was present in every country except Algeria and Libya, and it is likely a leftover from the ancient trade routes across the Indian Ocean. Haplogroup A was present in every country and may have come from commercial breeds. Haplogroup B was found only in Ethiopia. Haplogroup C was found only in the south-west of Saudi Arabia and in Ethiopia.

Conclusion

Our results support the idea that the Indian subcontinent had a major influence on the variety of mother's family lines in today's chickens. Most of the genetic variety lies within each population rather than between different populations. We also found no clear pattern in which family branches are found in which places. This fits with the idea that both ancient and more recent trade networks shaped the variety of local chickens across populations and countries.
parts.introduction_first: Village chickens are undoubtedly a valuable genetic resource for countries around the world. They are suited to their local surroundings, and they cope better with the diseases that are always present in their area. They provide high-quality protein and are a major source of income for poor communities. In this way, they do a great deal to help people have enough food, to reduce poverty and to look after natural resources [1]. Most local chickens are raised by letting them roam and find their own food, either by scavenging (searching for scraps and insects) or partly by scavenging. This way of raising them needs very little from the farmer. In the developing countries of Asia and Africa, it makes up as much as 80% of all the chickens kept [2].
parts.conclusion:
Conclusion

In this paper, we present for the first time the genetic variety of local chickens from Algeria, Iraq and Libya, using the DNA of their mothers' family lines (the D-loop). Together with what other studies have found, our results add further support to the idea that the chickens of the countries we studied mainly came from the Indian subcontinent. They also support the idea that the ancient trade routes across the Indian Ocean were important in spreading the species. However, overall we saw no clear pattern, or only a weak one, in which family branches are found in which places across the populations we studied. This shows that the D-loop, as a measure of genetic variety in chickens, has its limits when it comes to tracing where chickens came from.
parts.methods:
Methods

Collecting the samples and getting the DNA out

We studied 706 chicken samples in total. Of these, 92 came from Pakistan, 107 from Iraq, 23 from Libya, 185 from Saudi Arabia, 88 from Algeria and 211 from Ethiopia.

In Iraq, we collected samples from five different areas (Fig. 5) and sorted them into three groups. The first group was the North, with 9 samples from Sulimania in the north-east of the country. The second was the Central group, with two places in the middle of Iraq: 51 samples from Baghdad and 12 from Karbala. The third was the South, with two places in the south-east and south of the country: 24 samples from Misan and 11 from Basra.

In Saudi Arabia, we collected samples from 17 sites, again sorted into three groups. The East group had 45 samples from Al-Qatef, Hafar Al-Batin and Al-Hessa. The Central group had 43 samples from Hail, Al-Aflaj, Al-Kharj, Al-Amariah and Unayzah. The West group had 97 samples from Abha, Al-Baha, Jeddah, Jazan, Mecca, Medina, Najran, Tabuk and Taif.

In Algeria, the samples fell into two groups. The North group had 20 samples from Mascara, 17 from Oran, 11 from Tiaret and 18 from Tlemcen. The Central group had 22 samples from Adrar.

In Libya, the political situation meant we could only sample one population. It came from the north-west of the country, along the Mediterranean Sea.

Fig. 5

Where we collected samples, and how we grouped them by region, in each country

In Ethiopia, we collected chicken samples from 19 different sites, in both the highland and the lowland parts of the country. We examined ten samples from each site, except for four populations: 8 from Batambie, 30 from Horro, 14 from Jarso and 9 from Surta. We sorted the Ethiopian populations into four groups. The North group was Meseret and Mihquan. The Central-East group was Adane, Arabo, Horro, Jarso, Midir and Negasi Amba. The West group was Ashuda, Amshi, Batambie, Dikuli, Gafera, Surta and Tzion Teguaz. The South group was Kumato, Loya, Shubi Gemo and Girissa.

We took all the blood samples from village chickens that roam freely and search for scraps and insects, either fully or partly. We followed standard veterinary practice, which was approved by the authority in charge in each country. We also had the farmers' written or spoken agreement to sample their birds.

Getting the DNA out, copying it and lining it up

We stored the blood in two ways. Some was air-dried on special FTA classic cards (FTA® cards, made by Whatman Biosciences), which hold the DNA in place. For this blood, we took out the DNA with the MACHEREY-NAGEL DNA extraction kit. Other blood was kept whole in ethanol (a type of alcohol). For this, we used the Qiagen kit. In both cases, we followed the makers' instructions.

Next, we made many copies of the D-loop, a stretch of DNA 549 base pairs long. (A base pair is one "rung" of the DNA ladder, so this stretch is 549 letters long.) To copy it, we used a method called PCR (polymerase chain reaction). PCR copies one chosen piece of DNA over and over again. It needs two short starter pieces of DNA, called primers, that mark where copying begins and ends. Our forward primer was AV1F2 (5′-AGGACTACGGCTTGAAAAGC-3′) [15], and our reverse primer was H547 (5′- ATGTGCCTGACCGAGGAACCAG-3′) [16].

Each PCR reaction had a total volume of 20 μl (microlitres, millionths of a litre). It held 40 ng (billionths of a gram) of DNA, 10 μl of a ready-made PCR mix (Thermo Scientific Ltd), 0.5 μM of each primer, and sterile, nuclease-free water to bring the volume up to 20 μl.

We ran the PCR in a Peltier thermocycler, a machine that heats and cools the samples in a set pattern. The lid was kept hot at 110 °C. The machine started at 98 °C for 30 seconds. It then ran 35 cycles, each made of three steps: 98 °C for 5 seconds to pull the two strands of DNA apart, 63 °C for 5 seconds to let the primers attach, and 72 °C for 10 seconds to build the new copies. A final step at 72 °C for 1 minute finished the copies [17–19].

To check that the copying had worked, we ran the products through a 1% agarose gel, a jelly that sorts DNA pieces by size, at 100 V for 45 minutes. We then stained the gel with 1% ethidium bromide, a dye that makes DNA glow, and looked at it under ultraviolet light. To judge the size of the copied piece, we compared it with a "1 kb DNA ladder" from New England BioLabs, a set of DNA pieces of known sizes that we loaded alongside the PCR products. Finally, we cleaned up the products with the reSource PCR purification kit from Source Bioscience.

We read the order of the DNA letters using Sanger sequencing, a standard method for reading short stretches of DNA, on an Applied Biosystems 3730 DNA Analyser. For each sample, we used the program proseq3 (version 3.5) [20] to cut the sequence down to the 549-letter piece and to correct any mistakes in reading the letters. We then lined up each sequence against the known chicken D-loop sequence (GenBank number AB098668) [16], using the program Clustal X (version 2.1) [21]. Lining up sequences like this, so that matching positions sit side by side, is called alignment.

We only analysed the first 397 letters of the sequence. This part includes the most changeable section of the D-loop, called the hypervariable region (HV1) [22]. We added the sequences from all six countries to the public GenBank database (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/genbank/), under the numbers MK920994 to MK921699.

For all the Ethiopian samples, and for 22 of the Iraqi samples, we did not need to run PCR. Instead, we took the full D-loop from data that had already been used to read the chickens' whole DNA. For this, we used the Genome Analysis Toolkit (GATK V3.7) [23, 24]. We then lined up these sequences against the known chicken D-loop sequence and kept the same 397 letters for the rest of the analysis.

Measuring genetic variety

We used the program DnaSP v5 to find the positions in the DNA where chickens differed from one another. We also counted the number of haplotypes, which are the different versions of the D-loop sequence. In addition, we calculated three measures of genetic variety [25]. Haplotype diversity (Hd) shows how many different versions there are and how evenly they are spread. Nucleotide diversity (π) shows how much the DNA letters differ between versions, on average. The average number of nucleotide differences is the average number of letter differences between two versions. We worked out all of these for each population and for each country.

To test whether the differences in haplotype and nucleotide diversity between groups were statistically significant, we followed the method of Alexander et al. [26]. A difference is called statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone.

Building family trees

To see where the samples might have come from, we added reference sequences from the family branches (haplogroups) described by Liu et al. [14]. These were AB114069 for haplogroup A, AB007744 for B, AB114070 for C, AY588636 for D, AB114076 for E, AF512285 for F, AF512288 for G, D82904 for H and AB009434 for I.

We built a family tree of the sequences in two steps. First, the program jModeltest (version 2.1.7) [27] chose the model of DNA change that best fitted our data. Then the program Phyml (version 3.0) [28] built a maximum likelihood tree, which is the tree that best explains the DNA differences we see. To check how much we could trust each branch, we used 1000 bootstrap replications. In this test, the computer rebuilds the tree many times from reshuffled versions of the data and counts how often each branch appears again.

To show how the different versions of the D-loop are related, we also built a Median-Joining (MJ) network, a diagram that links versions by the fewest changes between them. We made it with the programs NETWORK 5.0.0 [29] and PopArt [30]. To show the ancient routes that chickens may have travelled along, we also downloaded 775 sequences from Chad, Egypt, Nigeria, Sudan, Turkey and Iran from GenBank (Table S1).

Measuring how much of the genetic variety lies within and between groups (AMOVA)

We used a method called analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) to split the genetic variety into two parts: the part found within each group and the part found between groups. We ran it in the program Arlequin v 3.5.2, with 1000 permutations [31]. Permutations means the computer shuffles the samples between groups many times to see how often a split this large appears by chance.

We ran the AMOVA in two ways. First, we compared countries, treating each country as one group and using all of its samples. Second, we compared groups within each country, using the groups described in the sampling section. The Iraqi samples were split into three groups: Central (63 samples), North (9) and South (35). The Algerian samples were split into two groups, North-West and Central. The Ethiopian samples were split into four groups: (Meseret and Mihquan), (Adane, Arabo, Horro, Jarso, Midir and Negasi Amba), (Ashuda, Amshi, Batambie, Dikuli, Gafera, Surta and Tzion Teguaz), and (Girissa, Kumato, Loya, Shubi Gemo). The Saudi Arabian samples were split into three groups: East (45 samples), Central (43) and West (97). All the Libyan samples were treated as one population, and so were all the Pakistani samples.

Testing for signs of past population changes

We worked out the population history of each population from its mismatch distribution [32]. A mismatch distribution is a chart showing how many DNA differences there are between each pair of samples. It can reveal whether a population has grown or shrunk over time. We compared the mismatch distribution we actually saw with the one we would expect, and calculated the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), the average size of the gap between the two. This gave us support for whether the population had expanded [33]. We then calculated two further tests, Fu's Fs [34] and Tajima's D [35], in DnaSP v.5 [25]. Both tests look for signs of a population that has grown quickly. They assume the infinite site model, the idea that each new mutation appears at a new position in the DNA.

To look more closely at the population history of the chickens within each country, we used Bayesian Skyline Plots (BSPs) [36]. A skyline plot is a graph that estimates how the size of a population has changed over time. We made them with the piecewise constant function in the program BEAST V 2.4.7 [37]. This function splits time into stretches and estimates a separate population size for each stretch.

First, we used the HKY + G model of DNA change, which allows different kinds of letter swaps to happen at different rates and some positions to change faster than others. We then ran a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulation. This is a computer method that takes a long series of small random steps to explore which answers fit the data best. We ran it separately for twenty million steps (called generations) and saved a result every one thousand steps. We threw away the first two million steps as "burn-in", because the simulation had not yet settled down.

We used the program Tracer V.1.7 [38] to check that the estimates of population size (Ne) had settled down and were no longer changing, which is called convergence. We then turned the skyline plots into time using the known rate of change for the chicken D-loop: 3.13 × 10− 7 mutations per site per year (m/s/y), following Alexander et al. [39]. We made these estimates for each country's samples separately and then plotted them together.
parts.results:
Results

### How many DNA versions we found, and how varied they were

In the 706 DNA sequences we read, we found 88 different versions of the D-loop (Additional file 1: Fig. S1). Each version differs from the others at 63 positions in the DNA where at least one chicken has a different letter. We call each version a haplotype, and we named them H_1, H_2, H_3 and so on.

The most common version was H_3, which turned up in 291 of the 706 sequences, or 41% of all the samples. Of the 92 Saudi sequences, 50% carried H_3. The same was true of 60 of the 60 Ethiopian sequences (100%), 58 of the 58 Iraqi sequences (100%), 55 of the 55 Algerian sequences (100%), 14 of the 14 Pakistani sequences (100%) and 12 of the 12 Libyan sequences (100%). The next most common versions were H_23 and H_4, found in 7.6% and 6% of all the sequences. Looking country by country, H_23 appeared only in Ethiopian samples (54 sequences, 26% of the Ethiopian samples), and H_4 appeared only in Pakistani chickens (43 sequences, 47% of the Pakistani samples).

To measure how varied the DNA was, we used two numbers. Haplotype diversity tells us how likely it is that two chickens picked at random carry different versions. Nucleotide diversity tells us how different the DNA letters are, on average, between two versions. For both, a higher number means more variety.

In Iraq, the Central region was much more varied than the North-East and the South. Its haplotype diversity was 0.725 ± 0.053 in Baghdad and 0.712 ± 0.105 in Karbala. In the South-East, Misan had 0.438 ± 0.121, and in the South, Basra had 0.182 ± 0.144 (Table 1 and Additional file 1: Table S2a). The number after the ± sign is the standard deviation, which shows how much the value could vary. The Central region was also more varied in its DNA letters, and this difference was statistically significant (P ≤ 0.05) and highly significant (P ≤ 0.001) (Additional file 1: Table S2b).

We call a difference statistically significant when, if there were really no difference, a gap this large would rarely appear by chance alone. For P ≤ 0.05, that means less than 5% of the time, and for P ≤ 0.001, less than 0.1% of the time.

In Algeria, three areas stood out. Adrar, Oran and Tlemcen had higher haplotype diversity (0.654 ± 0.085, 0.706 ± 0.106 and 0.797 ± 0.088) and higher nucleotide diversity (0.0035 ± 0.0006, 0.0022 ± 0.0005 and 0.00565 ± 0.0021) than Mascara and Tiaret, which had 0.363 ± 0.131 and 0.182 ± 0.144 and 0.001 ± 0.0004 and 0.0009 ± 0.0007.

Several pairs of areas differed significantly in haplotype diversity (P ≤ 0.05): Tlemcen and Tiaret, Tlemcen and Mascara, Adrar and Tiaret, and Oran and Tiaret (Additional file 1: Table S3a). For nucleotide diversity, we found only two significant differences (P ≤ 0.001 and P ≤ 0.05). One was between Mascara and Tlemcen, and the other was between Tiaret and Tlemcen (Additional file 1: Table S3b).

In Ethiopia, different populations had different levels of variety. Adane, Arabo, Kumato, Loya, Meseret and Shubi had haplotype diversity that was highly significant (P ≤ 0.001) or significant (P ≤ 0.05) (Additional file 1: Table S4a). In these same populations, nucleotide diversity ranged from 0.0033 to 0.0145, with highly significant (P ≤ 0.001) or significant (P ≤ 0.05) differences between populations (Additional file 1: Table S4b). When we compared the three regions, the North, Central-East and West did not differ significantly from one another. The South, however, had the most genetic variety of all the regions.

The regions of Saudi Arabia also differed significantly in how varied they were (Additional file 1: S5a). Haplotype diversity was highest in the East, on the shores of the Arabian Gulf (0.856 ± 0.044), next highest in the West, on the shores of the Red Sea (0.702 ± 0.041), and lowest in the Central region (0.631 ± 0.084). For nucleotide diversity, we found no significant differences within Saudi Arabia (Additional file 1: Table S5b). Libya and Pakistan both had high variety, with haplotype diversity of 0.731 ± 0.099 and 0.756 ± 0.043 and nucleotide diversity of 0.0054 ± 0.0018 and 0.0088 ± 0.001.

Comparing whole countries, Ethiopia had the highest haplotype diversity and Algeria the lowest. Iraq, Libya, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia fell in between.

### Tracing the family branches and where they are found

We used reference haplotypes from Liu et al. [14] to name the family branches (haplogroups) using their naming system: a, B, C, D, E, F, G, H and I. To see how the 88 versions are related, we built a family tree of them using a method called maximum likelihood (Fig. 1). This method picks the tree that best explains the DNA differences we see. To check how much we can trust each branch, we used bootstrap values. These show how often a branch reappears when the data are resampled many times, so a value of 100 means the branch appeared every time. Most branches had high bootstrap values, between 70 and 100, and together they suggest five family branches: a, B, C, D and E.

We sorted the versions into family branches using the tree and a network, both for all the countries together and for each country on its own (Figs. 1 and 2, Additional file 1: Figs. S2 to S7). A network is a diagram that links DNA versions by the number of DNA changes between them. Table 2 shows how many samples of each version came from each country.

Haplogroup E was by far the most common, with 625 of the 706 chickens. Next came D (46 chickens), a (31), C (3) and B (1). Haplogroup a was made up of 7 versions, B of one, C of two and D of 11.

Network of the versions from Algeria, Ethiopia, Iraq, Libya, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, built with the median-joining method. Black circles are reference versions. Haplogroup E was present in very different numbers of chickens in the six countries. Out of the 625 chickens that carried it, 87 were in Algeria (99%), 169 in Ethiopia (80%), 84 in Iraq (79%), 21 in Libya (91%), 84 in Pakistan (91%) and 180 in Saudi Arabia (97%).

Haplogroup A was found in 31 samples, spread across all the countries. Haplogroups B and C were found only in Ethiopia and Saudi Arabia. One version from Ethiopia was identical to the reference version B. Haplogroup C was made up of one Ethiopian version and one Saudi version, the latter from two samples in the South-West region.

Haplogroup D was present in every country except Algeria and Libya. It was made up of eleven versions, plus the reference version. Of the 46 chickens that carried it, 34 were in Ethiopia (16%), 8 in Iraq (7%), 3 in Pakistan (7%) and 1 in Saudi Arabia (0.5%).

The network shows the variety of the versions and how they are related in a way the tree does not. The most common versions, H_3, H_4 and H_23, all belong to haplogroup E (Fig. 2). H_3 is identical to the reference version. H_4 differs from H_3 by only 4 DNA changes, and H_23 differs from H_3 by just one.

The links between haplogroup E and the other family branches are clear. Haplogroup E is separated from haplogroup D by several DNA changes, with three median vectors. A median vector is a link in the network that stands for a version we did not sample but that must have existed to connect the versions we did. Haplogroup C is connected to E by 12 DNA changes and 5 median vectors. The other groups are linked in the same way, except for haplogroup F, which was connected to E by 7 DNA changes with no median vectors. The median vectors may point to versions that were never sampled, for example versions that never reached the area, or versions that have died out [15]. H_3, from haplogroup E, sits at the centre of a star-like pattern, so it is likely the ancestral version of this family branch.

We also downloaded reference sequences from other studies and built trees and networks for them (Additional file 1: Figs. S8 and S9). These gave results similar to those for our own samples: the same family branches (A, B, C, D and E) and a similar pattern of where the versions are found.

### How the genetic variety is split between groups (AMOVA)

We used a method called analysis of molecular variance (AMOVA) to see how the genetic variety in our samples is split between groups (Table 3). It works out what share of all the genetic variety lies between groups, between populations within groups, and between individual chickens within populations. We looked at three levels: groups (regions within a country), populations within groups, and individual chickens within populations.

In Iraq and Algeria, most of the variety lay between individual chickens within populations: 66.33% in Iraq and 94.41% in Algeria. The share between groups was higher in Iraq (28.89%) than in Algeria (5.03%). In Ethiopia, a fairly large share lay between populations within groups (45.84%) and between individual chickens within populations (42.87%), with less between groups (11.29%). In Saudi Arabia, most of the variety (96.66%) lay between individual chickens within regions, and hardly any (3.34%) lay between regions. When we compared all six countries together (Algeria, Ethiopia, Iraq, Libya, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia), the largest share was between individual chickens within populations (74.12%), followed by between populations within countries (17.01%).

### Population history and changes in population size

We looked at the population history of each population and each country using several measures. The first was the mean absolute error (MAE), which shows how well a model of population history fits the data. Its values were moderate to low (Table 4).

The second was Tajima's D, a test that compares two different ways of measuring genetic variety. A negative value means there are more rare DNA versions than expected. This can happen when a population has grown, after a bottleneck (a sharp drop in numbers) or a selective sweep (when a helpful gene spreads and carries nearby DNA along with it). It can also happen through purifying selection, when harmful DNA changes are weeded out. For many populations, Tajima's D was negative but not statistically significant. The exceptions were Misan, Mascara, Tiaret, Tlemcen, North-West Algeria, the South region of Iraq, Libya, and the East, Central and West regions of Saudi Arabia, where Tajima's D was negative and significant.

The third was Fu's Fs, another test of population growth that is known to be more powerful than Tajima's D [40]. Its strength comes from its ability to tell population growth apart from genetic hitchhiking, where DNA changes spread because they sit next to a helpful gene, and from rejecting the idea that the DNA changes are neutral, meaning they do not affect survival.

The fourth was the Harpending raggedness index (r), which checks whether the pattern of DNA differences fits a population that has grown. It was not significant for any population except the Algerian samples when they were grouped together.

Taken together, these results suggest a complex population history for our chickens. We also used two more methods to look for signs of past population growth. The first, the mismatch distribution, counts how many DNA changes separate each pair of sequences. The second, the Bayesian skyline plot (BSP), estimates how the effective population size (roughly, the number of breeding chickens) changed over time.

Discussion

In this study, we looked at the genetic variety of the D-loop, the stretch of DNA passed down from mothers, in 706 village chickens from Algeria, Ethiopia, Iraq, Libya, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. Our aim was to work out the chickens' history and where they came from. As far as we know, this is the first study of the D-loop in local chickens from Algeria, Iraq and Libya. For Ethiopia, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia, other studies have already reported information about different populations that we did not include here [15, 41, 42].

The history of how people first tamed chickens is still unsettled. The Indian subcontinent and South-East Asia have both been suggested as major places where the domestic chicken first came from. For the Indian subcontinent, the Indus Valley is one possible centre. If so, we would expect Pakistani chickens to have the most variety in their D-loop. That is not what we found when we looked at all the family branches together for each country (Table 1). It is also not what we found when we looked only at haplogroup E (Additional file 1: Table S6). This branch is thought to have its centre of variety on the Indian subcontinent, and Liu et al. [14] reported it as the most common one in Europe and India.

Whether we looked at all the family branches or only haplogroup E, Ethiopia had the most variety. This may be because of how many chickens we examined: we had more than twice as many Ethiopian samples as Pakistani ones. Or, on top of that, it may reflect chickens arriving in East Africa several times, by different routes.

Interestingly, earlier studies have suggested that the chickens of East Africa may have come from two different places [15, 43]. One part came by land from the Indian subcontinent. Another part came from South-East Asian chickens, which travelled by sea along trading routes across the Indian Ocean. The second most common family branch, haplogroup D, is thought to be a leftover from these past Indian Ocean trading networks [14]. We often found this branch in Ethiopian samples (Table 2), and it was more common in the southern region. It was completely missing in Libya and Algeria, and it appeared, but only rarely, in Iraq, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia. This pattern across the map fits with the branch spreading by sea across the Indian Ocean.

The branch was also missing in Algeria and Libya, and it was fairly rare in the other countries. Together with where it is found in Ethiopia, this suggests that haplogroup D may have arrived and spread after haplogroup E had already spread north and west.

Within each country, the amount of variety differed from one region to another. In Iraq, chickens from the central area had more variety than the two populations from the south of the country (Table 1). The high variety in the central region may be because chickens reached the country by land through the inland route, rather than by sea in the south. It is also worth remembering that the central area includes the capital, Baghdad, a city built in the eighth century as the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate. So, over time, this region may have seen large movements of people and their livestock from different parts of the world. Another possibility is that chickens reached today's Iraq by a sea trading route, and that the populations then mixed more recently.

In Algeria, we found only haplogroup E, apart from one DNA version that belonged to haplogroup A. The variety in the northern part of the country was nearly the same as in the more central region. The populations we studied live close to each other, so this result might not be surprising. To find out whether Algerian chickens form a single genetic group, we need to study other populations from other parts of the country.

In Libya, we studied only one population. As in Algeria, we found only two family branches, and haplogroup E was the most common. Taken together, these results support the idea that the chickens of these two countries, and by extension of the shores of the Mediterranean Sea, mainly came from the Indian subcontinent. They may have travelled inland through the Fertile Crescent, the fertile land of the Middle East, or by a more direct route through the Red Sea and Egypt.

In Saudi Arabia, we found four family branches (A, C, D and E), with E the most common. This probably reflects more than one route by which chickens were brought into the country, and more than one origin. Haplogroup E probably came from the Indian subcontinent by land and by sea. The other branches may have reached the country through the sea trading networks of the Arabian Gulf and the Red Sea. The variety we measured in the different regions supports this further. The eastern part, on the Arabian Gulf, had higher variety (0.856 ± 0.044) than the central (0.631 ± 0.084) and western (0.702 ± 0.041) regions of the country.

In Ethiopia, we found five family branches (A, B, C, D and E), which may have arrived in different ways. As we mentioned earlier, haplogroup E, the most common, probably came from the Indian subcontinent. It may have travelled by land along the Nile River Basin, or it may have arrived through the coastal areas of the Horn of Africa, or both. The second most common branch, D, most likely came by sea.

Within Ethiopia, the southern region had the highest variety, both in its DNA versions (0.929 ± 0.021) and in its nucleotide variety, which measures how often the DNA letters differ between samples (0.0150 ± 0.0006). The other three Ethiopian regions had less. The central-east, north and west regions were similar to each other.

Compared with other studies, the D-loop variety in Ethiopian, Iraqi, Libyan, Pakistani and Saudi chickens is higher than what earlier studies reported for chickens from Iran, Turkey and Egypt [44–46]. In the same way, among the chicken populations studied before in Africa south of the Sahara, the countries in our study had more genetic variety than populations from Nigeria, Chad, Uganda and Sudan [15, 22, 47]. These results need to be read with care, because we studied different numbers of samples. Even so, in these other countries haplogroup E is still by far the most common, and the other branches are either rare or missing. This supports our earlier conclusion that haplogroup E reached the African continent before the other branches.

The high variety in the D-loop of Ethiopian chickens reflects the large movements of livestock in the past, along the trading routes that linked Ethiopia to the civilisations of the Fertile Crescent. It also shows how important the Horn of Africa was as a place where livestock entered the continent.

One DNA version, called H_3, was very common in every country we studied (Fig. 2). It probably represents an ancestral version of haplogroup E. Most samples fell into haplogroup E, while haplogroups A, B, C and D were found only rarely. Haplogroups E and A were found in all the countries we studied. Haplogroup B was found only in Ethiopia, in just one chicken from the Mihquan population. Haplogroup C was present only in Saudi Arabian and Ethiopian samples. In Saudi Arabia, it was found in the south-west, on the shores of the Red Sea (Abhaa and Jazan), and in Ethiopia it was found in the south (Loya).

Haplogroups A and B have been reported before, mainly from South China [14]. Haplogroup C was first seen in chickens from Japan and South-East China, which spread through the ancient sea trading network [14]. Where these rare branches in our samples came from is only a guess. They may be leftovers from ancient spread, or they may come from more recent crossbreeding with commercial breeds, or both.

Overall, we used a method called AMOVA (analysis of molecular variance), which splits the genetic variety into parts: the part found between countries, the part found between populations within a country, and the part found between individual chickens within a population. It showed that the countries were similar, and that most of the variety was found between individual chickens within populations (Table 3). However, Ethiopia and Iraq showed more variety between populations within their countries than the other countries did. This supports how we interpreted the DNA versions and family branches above, and in particular for Ethiopia it suggests that chickens arrived by several routes. It also shows that, once chickens reached a country, they bred with each other and mixed their genes. This limits how useful the D-loop is as a genetic marker for tracing where chickens came from within a single country.
